subChunks.title: Defining & Classifying Mental Illness
subChunks.hookHtml:
In 1973, the American Psychiatric Association removed homosexuality from its diagnostic manual — not because new research had emerged, but after sustained political pressure and a membership vote. The decision illustrates something fundamental: the classification of psychological abnormality is not purely a scientific enterprise. It reflects the values, assumptions, and power structures of the societies that produce diagnostic systems.

Yet psychiatric diagnosis is also a clinical and scientific tool with genuine utility — enabling communication between clinicians, informing treatment selection, facilitating research, and providing individuals with a framework for understanding their experiences. The challenge is holding both truths simultaneously.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Defining Abnormality

No single definition of psychological abnormality is fully satisfactory. Four main criteria have been proposed, each capturing something important while failing in specific cases.

Statistical infrequency: abnormality is defined as deviation from the statistical norm. Simple, objective, and culturally neutral in principle. Problems: intellectual giftedness is statistically rare but not disordered; depression is statistically common in many populations but clearly abnormal. Frequency alone cannot determine clinical significance.

Violation of social norms: behaviours that transgress culturally accepted standards are abnormal. Problems: norms are culturally and historically relative (as homosexuality illustrates); this criterion risks pathologising dissent or non-conformity.

Failure to function adequately: Rosenhan & Seligman (1989) proposed a cluster of criteria including personal distress, maladaptiveness, unpredictability, irrationality, observer discomfort, and violation of moral standards. More clinically sensitive than statistical infrequency, but subjective — functioning is culturally defined and varies by context (e.g., a soldier in combat).

Deviation from ideal mental health: Jahoda (1958) proposed positive criteria for mental health: self-actualisation, integration, autonomy, reality perception, environmental mastery, and positive self-regard. Rarely used clinically because few people meet all criteria — the threshold pathologises the majority of the population.

Classification Systems

The two dominant classification systems are the DSM-5-TR (Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, fifth edition, text revision; American Psychiatric Association, 2022) and the ICD-11 (International Classification of Diseases, 11th revision; World Health Organization, 2022). The DSM uses categorical diagnosis (a condition is either present or absent, based on symptom threshold criteria) and organises disorders into chapters by symptom cluster.

DSM-5 moved from a multi-axial system (Axes I–V) to a dimensional approach in some areas (e.g., autism spectrum disorder on a severity spectrum; personality disorder dimensions). ICD-11 has moved further toward dimensionality, particularly for personality disorders.

Key criticisms of categorical diagnosis: comorbidity is very high — the majority of individuals meeting criteria for one disorder also meet criteria for another, suggesting the boundaries between categories are artificial. Heterogeneity within categories — two individuals with major depressive disorder may share only one symptom. Reliability concerns: Rosenhan's (1973) 'On Being Sane in Insane Places' study demonstrated that pseudo-patients admitting one symptom were hospitalised for extended periods and discharged with 'in remission' diagnoses, suggesting clinicians' diagnostic perception is influenced by context and labelling. Inter-rater reliability for DSM diagnoses, while improved since DSM-III, remains imperfect for some categories (e.g., personality disorders: κ = 0.21–0.54 in DSM-5 field trials).

The Medical Model and its Critics

The medical model conceptualises mental illness as analogous to physical illness: discrete diseases with biological aetiology, specific symptoms, and targeted treatments. This model underpins psychiatric classification and drives pharmacological research. Thomas Szasz (1960) famously argued that mental illness is a 'myth' — that psychiatry medicalises moral and social deviance, and that psychiatric diagnosis is a mechanism of social control. Szasz's position is widely considered too extreme, but it generated productive critiques of psychiatric power. The biopsychosocial model (Engel, 1977) offers a more nuanced framework: biological, psychological, and social factors interact to produce, maintain, and modify mental health difficulties — a perspective increasingly reflected in clinical guidelines.

storyBeats.text: Dr. Chen projects a timeline on the screen: 1952 (DSM-I published), 1973 (homosexuality removed), 1980 (DSM-III: reliability revolution), 1994 (DSM-IV), 2013 (DSM-5: dimensional shift).

storyBeats.speaker: Dr. Chen
storyBeats.text: Every edition of the DSM adds and removes diagnoses. Grief was, until 2013, a reason to not diagnose major depression — the 'bereavement exclusion'. DSM-5 removed it. Suddenly, profound grief lasting more than two weeks could meet criteria for a mood disorder. Is that a scientific finding or a cultural decision?
She shows the kappa reliability coefficients from DSM-5 field trials. Some categories — major depression, bipolar I — show good agreement. Personality disorders sit far lower.

storyBeats.speaker: Dr. Chen
storyBeats.text: Reliability is the precondition for validity. If two clinicians can't agree on whether someone has borderline personality disorder, what does that diagnosis actually mean? The DSM-5 field trials were honest enough to publish those coefficients. Previous editions weren't.

storyBeats.speaker: Dr. Chen
storyBeats.text: The medical model has real clinical utility. It drives pharmacological research, enables insurance reimbursement, gives people a name for their experience. But it can also obscure the social causes of distress — poverty, trauma, discrimination — by locating the problem entirely within the individual. A diagnosis is a tool, not a truth.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Guided Practice — Critiquing the DSM

Scenario: A clinical psychologist is presenting to a team about a new patient. She describes the patient as 'a 34-year-old woman presenting with comorbid major depressive disorder, generalised anxiety disorder, and borderline personality disorder'. A trainee psychiatrist asks: 'If she meets criteria for three separate disorders, doesn't that suggest the diagnostic boundaries between them might be artificial?'

Using your knowledge of the DSM classification system and its critics, evaluate the trainee's challenge. In your answer, explain the problem of high comorbidity for categorical diagnosis, consider what alternatives (dimensional approaches) have been proposed, and reach a balanced conclusion about the clinical utility of diagnosis versus its theoretical limitations.

Guidance: Define comorbidity and explain why it is theoretically problematic before evaluating. Aim for 120–150 words.
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
The trainee raises a fundamental critique of the DSM's categorical approach. Comorbidity—the simultaneous presence of multiple diagnoses—is the rule rather than the exception in psychiatric practice. When a patient meets criteria for major depression, generalised anxiety, and borderline personality disorder simultaneously, it strongly suggests that these are not discrete, natural disease entities, but rather overlapping symptom clusters with shared underlying aetiologies (such as negative affectivity).

Dimensional approaches, such as the Five Factor Model or the HiTOP framework, address this by conceptualising psychopathology as continuous traits rather than binary categories. Instead of multiple comorbid diagnoses, the patient would be described by a profile of symptom dimensions (e.g., severe negative emotionality and dysregulation).

However, despite these theoretical limitations, categorical diagnosis retains clinical utility. It provides a shared shorthand for clinicians, facilitates treatment selection, and enables access to services. The optimal approach acknowledges categorical diagnoses as useful heuristics rather than definitive biological boundaries.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
Independent Practice — Definitions of Abnormality

A clinical team is assessing three individuals for possible psychological intervention: (1) a professional tightrope walker who shows no apparent anxiety while performing at great heights, which is statistically uncommon and violates most people's intuitions about rational risk; (2) a person experiencing severe depression who reports that their sadness feels entirely appropriate given their recent bereavement; (3) a woman in a culture that practices extensive fasting for religious reasons, whose caloric intake would meet diagnostic criteria for an eating disorder if assessed by Western standards.

Using at least three definitions of abnormality (statistical infrequency, social norms, failure to function adequately, deviation from ideal mental health), evaluate how each definition applies to each case. Consider the limitations that each case exposes. Reach a conclusion about which definition, or combination of definitions, is most clinically useful.

Write at least 150 words in paragraphs. This is an evaluative task — reach clear conclusions, do not merely describe each definition.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
The three cases systematically expose the limitations of each definition of abnormality when applied uncritically.

The tightrope walker challenges statistical infrequency as a definition: his absence of fear at height is statistically rare, but classifying him as abnormal because he lacks a common anxiety response conflates uncommon with disordered. Statistical infrequency cannot distinguish pathology from exceptional competence, rendering it insufficient as a standalone criterion.

The bereaved depressed person challenges the failure to function adequately criterion. They may report that their sadness is meaningful and that they are, in a sense, functioning as they should be in response to loss — grief is culturally prescribed. Rosenhan & Seligman's (1989) criterion of personal distress is more sensitive here: if the person is significantly distressed and their daily functioning is impaired, clinical attention may be warranted regardless of subjective attribution.

The fasting woman most sharply exposes the problem with social norms as a definition. Her behaviour is culturally normative within her context; a definition of abnormality based on Western medical norms would pathologise a widespread religious practice. This illustrates the cultural relativity of all norm-based criteria and raises serious questions about the cross-cultural validity of DSM diagnostic thresholds.

No single definition is sufficient. The most clinically useful approach is a combination: the failure to function adequately criterion, supplemented by distress and cultural context, comes closest to capturing clinical need without over-pathologising difference. This aligns with the biopsychosocial model's recognition that abnormality must be understood within social and cultural context, not imposed from a culturally specific normative standard.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a school student why defining 'abnormality' in psychology is harder than it sounds. Give an example that shows why at least one common definition — like statistical infrequency — fails on its own.

The degree of agreement between different clinicians applying the same diagnostic criteria to the same case. Measured by Cohen's kappa (κ); essential for a diagnosis to be clinically meaningful.

Engel's (1977) framework proposing that mental health difficulties arise from the interaction of biological, psychological, and social factors — as opposed to the purely biological focus of the medical model.

A definition of abnormality proposed by Rosenhan & Seligman (1989) that focuses on personal distress, maladaptiveness, and impaired daily functioning as criteria, rather than statistical rarity alone.
Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, 5th edition, text revision (APA, 2022). The dominant psychiatric classification system in North America and much of the world.

subChunks.title: Anxiety, Mood & Psychotic Disorders
subChunks.hookHtml:
Three of the most prevalent and disabling mental health conditions globally — anxiety disorders, mood disorders, and psychotic disorders — differ dramatically in their phenomenology, aetiology, and treatment. Yet they share something fundamental: each is a disorder of how the mind processes and responds to itself and the world, with profound consequences for every domain of a person's life.

Understanding the psychological and biological mechanisms underlying these conditions — and the evidence for treatments targeting those mechanisms — is central to clinical psychology, psychiatry, and public mental health.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Anxiety Disorders

Anxiety disorders are the most prevalent mental health conditions globally (WHO, 2017), characterised by excessive, persistent fear or worry disproportionate to actual threat. DSM-5 separates generalised anxiety disorder (GAD), panic disorder, specific phobias, social anxiety disorder, and agoraphobia as distinct categories.

The cognitive model of anxiety (Beck et al., 1985) proposes that anxiety arises from biased information processing: attentional bias (selective attention to threat-relevant stimuli), interpretive bias (ambiguous information interpreted as threatening), and memory bias (better recall of threat-relevant material). The maintenance of anxiety involves safety behaviours (actions designed to prevent feared outcomes that prevent disconfirmation of threat beliefs) and avoidance (preventing exposure to feared stimuli).

Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT) is the most robustly evidenced psychological treatment for anxiety disorders. CBT targets maladaptive cognitions (cognitive restructuring) and avoidance (behavioural exposure). Clark's (1986) cognitive model of panic identifies catastrophic misinterpretation of bodily sensations (e.g., heart pounding interpreted as heart attack) as the maintaining mechanism; treatment involves exposure to sensations plus cognitive restructuring. Meta-analyses (Norton & Price, 2007) confirm CBT effectiveness across anxiety disorder subtypes.

Mood Disorders

Major depressive disorder (MDD) is characterised by persistent low mood, anhedonia, cognitive symptoms (negative automatic thoughts, hopelessness), somatic symptoms, and functional impairment. It is the leading cause of years lived with disability worldwide (GBD Collaborators, 2017).

Theoretical models: Beck's (1967) cognitive triad proposes that depression involves negative automatic thoughts about the self ('I am worthless'), the world ('Everything is hard'), and the future ('Nothing will improve'). These cognitions are maintained by cognitive errors (overgeneralisation, catastrophising, selective abstraction) and underlying negative schemas activated by life events. The learned helplessness model (Seligman, 1975; reformulated by Abramson, Seligman & Teasdale, 1978 as the attribution/hopelessness model) proposes that depression follows from an internal, stable, global attribution style for negative events — predicting helplessness and hopelessness.

Biological accounts emphasise the monoamine hypothesis (norepinephrine and serotonin deficiency), though as Moncrieff et al. (2022) comprehensively documented, evidence for a simple serotonin deficiency in depression is weak; the mechanisms of antidepressant action remain incompletely understood. Bipolar disorder involves episodes of both mania (elevated mood, reduced sleep, grandiosity, impulsive behaviour) and depression, with distinct neurobiological underpinnings and treatment (mood stabilisers including lithium).

Psychotic Disorders

Schizophrenia spectrum disorders are characterised by a combination of positive symptoms (experiences added to normal experience: hallucinations, delusions, disorganised thought) and negative symptoms (diminution of normal experience: flat affect, alogia, avolition, anhedonia). DSM-5 requires two or more symptoms for ≥1 month, with a significant impact on functioning for ≥6 months.

The dopamine hypothesis (Carlsson & Lindqvist, 1963) proposed that positive symptoms arise from hyperactivity of dopaminergic transmission in mesolimbic pathways. Evidence: drugs that block D2 receptors (antipsychotics) reduce positive symptoms; drugs that increase dopamine (amphetamine) can induce psychosis-like states. The revised dopamine hypothesis (Kapur, 2003) proposes that aberrant dopamine salience — the excessive motivational salience attributed to irrelevant stimuli — underlies delusion formation.

Psychological models: Garety et al.'s (2001) cognitive model of psychosis proposes that psychosocial stress activates a biological vulnerability, producing anomalous experiences; negative self-schemas and reasoning biases (particularly jumping to conclusions — the tendency to make decisions on insufficient evidence) drive delusion formation and maintenance. Psychological therapies for psychosis (CBTp) have demonstrated moderate effectiveness for positive symptoms (Wykes et al., 2008 meta-analysis).

storyBeats.text: Dr. Chen begins with a global burden statistic: 264 million people worldwide live with depression; 45 million with a psychotic disorder. She lets the numbers sit.

storyBeats.speaker: Dr. Chen
storyBeats.text: Aaron Beck developed his cognitive model of depression not from grand theory but from clinical observation. He noticed that his depressed patients had streams of spontaneous negative thoughts — he called them automatic thoughts. He started writing them down, categorising them. The cognitive triad came from that clinical work.
She shows a slide from Beck (1967): a triangle labelled SELF / WORLD / FUTURE, each vertex negative.

storyBeats.speaker: Dr. Chen
storyBeats.text: The dopamine hypothesis for schizophrenia tells a similar story — elegant, influential, and incomplete. Antipsychotics block D2 receptors and reduce positive symptoms. So dopamine must be involved. But which dopamine circuits, in which direction, producing which experiences? The original hypothesis was too simple. Kapur's salience model in 2003 was a significant refinement.

storyBeats.speaker: Dr. Chen
storyBeats.text: What all three disorder groups share is a bidirectional relationship between cognition and affect. Fear produces threat-focused thinking, which amplifies fear. Hopeless thinking suppresses motivation, deepening depression. Anomalous experience prompts explanation-seeking, and a person under stress who already has a negative self-schema will reach for threatening explanations first.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Guided Practice — Beck's Cognitive Triad in Context

Scenario: Ibrahim is a 28-year-old who was made redundant three months ago. He has become increasingly withdrawn, telling friends: 'I failed at the only job I was good at — I'll never find another one, and I'm a burden to everyone around me.' He no longer feels pleasure in activities he previously enjoyed and has difficulty getting out of bed before noon.

Using Beck's (1967) cognitive model of depression (cognitive triad and cognitive errors), analyse Ibrahim's presentation. Identify at least two cognitive errors in his thinking, explain how the cognitive model accounts for the maintenance of his depression, and briefly outline how CBT would target these maintaining factors.

Guidance: Quote or closely paraphrase Ibrahim's statements when identifying cognitive errors. Aim for 120–150 words.
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
Ibrahim's presentation exemplifies Beck’s (1967) cognitive triad: negative thoughts about the self ("I'm a burden"), the world ("I failed at the only job I was good at"), and the future ("I'll never find another one"). These thoughts are sustained by cognitive errors. Claiming he will *never* find another job is an example of *overgeneralisation* or *fortune-telling*. Concluding he is a burden based solely on being unemployed exemplifies *magnification* or *arbitrary inference*.

According to the cognitive model, these biased appraisals maintain his depression by generating feelings of hopelessness and anhedonia, which drive behavioural withdrawal (staying in bed). This withdrawal prevents him from encountering disconfirming evidence or experiencing positive reinforcement, further entrenching his negative beliefs in a vicious cycle.

Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT) would target these maintaining factors through cognitive restructuring—helping Ibrahim identify, evaluate, and challenge his negative automatic thoughts—and behavioural activation—scheduling graded activities to increase his engagement with the world and counteract his withdrawal.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
Independent Practice — Evaluating the Dopamine Hypothesis

The dopamine hypothesis (Carlsson & Lindqvist, 1963) has been the dominant biological account of schizophrenia for over sixty years. It generated antipsychotic pharmacology that transformed the lives of millions. Yet critics argue that it cannot account for key features of the disorder and that antipsychotics work imperfectly — negative symptoms respond poorly, 30% of patients are treatment-resistant, and the hypothesis does not explain the cognitive deficits that often precede positive symptoms by years.

Critically evaluate the original dopamine hypothesis and Kapur's (2003) revised 'aberrant salience' model. In your answer, consider the evidence supporting each account, the limitations both face, and whether psychological models (such as Garety et al.'s cognitive model) offer complementary explanatory value. Reach a conclusion about the current state of our understanding of schizophrenia's aetiology.

Write at least 150 words in paragraphs. Evaluate, do not merely describe.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
The original dopamine hypothesis (Carlsson & Lindqvist, 1963) rests on two compelling pillars: drugs blocking D2 receptors reduce positive symptoms, and dopamine-enhancing drugs (e.g., amphetamine) can induce psychosis-like states. However, the hypothesis cannot account for several key features. Clozapine — the most effective antipsychotic for treatment-resistant cases — has relatively low D2 affinity, acting instead on multiple receptor systems (serotonin, histamine, cholinergic). Negative symptoms — anhedonia, flat affect, alogia — and cognitive deficits respond poorly or not at all to D2 blockade, suggesting these features involve non-dopaminergic mechanisms (glutamate dysfunction, prefrontal hypofrontality).

Kapur's (2003) aberrant salience model is a significant theoretical advance. Rather than proposing global dopamine excess, it specifies that mesolimbic dopamine dysregulation drives the attribution of excessive motivational salience to irrelevant stimuli — producing the anomalous perceptual experiences and sense of meaning that the person then explains through delusional beliefs. This accounts more precisely for how positive symptoms develop rather than merely correlating with dopamine levels.

Garety et al.'s (2001) cognitive model complements rather than replaces the biological account. It explains individual differences in symptom expression: a person with a negative self-schema who experiences anomalous perceptions due to dopamine dysregulation will — given a jumping-to-conclusions reasoning bias — arrive at a threatening explanatory delusion faster and hold it more tenaciously than someone without these cognitive risk factors. The CBTp evidence base (Wykes et al., 2008) demonstrates that targeting these cognitive maintaining factors produces modest but significant symptom improvement, even in the absence of biological change.

The current state of understanding is one of informed pluralism: schizophrenia is almost certainly heterogeneous in aetiology, and an integrated biopsychosocial account — acknowledging dopaminergic mechanisms, glutamate systems, social adversity (childhood trauma increases psychosis risk threefold; Varese et al., 2012), and cognitive maintaining factors — better reflects the evidence than any single-level model.

Actions performed in anxiety-provoking situations to prevent feared outcomes (e.g., avoiding eye contact to prevent embarrassment). They maintain anxiety by preventing disconfirmation of threat beliefs.

The theory that positive symptoms of schizophrenia arise from hyperactivity of dopaminergic transmission in mesolimbic pathways, supported by antipsychotic drug action and stimulant-induced psychosis.

subChunks.title: Personality Disorders
subChunks.hookHtml:
Personality disorders sit at the most contested frontier of psychiatric classification. They describe enduring, pervasive patterns of inner experience and behaviour that deviate markedly from cultural expectations — patterns that, by definition, are not transient symptoms but the structure of a person's way of being in the world. Critics ask whether this is a coherent clinical concept or a covert moral judgement; advocates argue that without it, clinicians lose a crucial framework for understanding individuals whose suffering manifests in their relationships, identity, and self-regulation.

The debate matters profoundly. A diagnosis of borderline or antisocial personality disorder still carries stigma — including, distressingly, among clinicians themselves — and shapes access to care for decades. Getting the science right is an ethical imperative.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
The DSM-5 Cluster System

DSM-5 retains a categorical model of personality disorders (PDs), organising ten distinct diagnoses into three clusters based on descriptive similarity. Cluster A (odd or eccentric) includes paranoid PD (pervasive distrust and suspiciousness), schizoid PD (detachment from social relationships and restricted emotional expression), and schizotypal PD (eccentric behaviour, cognitive distortions, social discomfort — considered part of the schizophrenia spectrum). Cluster B (dramatic, emotional, or erratic) comprises antisocial PD (disregard for and violation of the rights of others), borderline PD (instability of relationships, self-image, and affect), narcissistic PD (grandiosity, need for admiration, lack of empathy), and histrionic PD (excessive emotionality and attention-seeking). Cluster C (anxious or fearful) covers avoidant PD (social inhibition and feelings of inadequacy), dependent PD (excessive need to be cared for), and obsessive-compulsive PD (preoccupation with orderliness and control — distinct from OCD).

The Categorical-Dimensional Debate

The categorical approach has been extensively criticised. Diagnostic comorbidity within and across clusters is extremely high; arbitrary symptom thresholds produce qualitatively similar individuals on either side of a diagnostic boundary; and personality traits clearly vary dimensionally in non-clinical populations. The Five Factor Model (FFM; Costa & McCrae, 1992) demonstrates that the same trait dimensions (neuroticism, extraversion, openness, agreeableness, conscientiousness) account for both normal personality variation and PD presentations, with PDs representing extreme positions on these continua.

DSM-5 includes an Alternative Model for Personality Disorders (AMPD) in Section III, combining impairment in personality functioning (self and interpersonal) with five pathological trait domains (negative affectivity, detachment, antagonism, disinhibition, psychoticism). Crucially, ICD-11 (WHO, 2022) has gone further, abandoning the categorical system entirely in favour of a fully dimensional model: clinicians rate severity (mild, moderate, severe) and may specify trait qualifiers, with borderline pattern retained as the sole categorical specifier in response to clinical demand.

Borderline Personality Disorder

BPD is characterised by emotional dysregulation, identity disturbance, unstable intense relationships, impulsivity, suicidality, dissociation, and chronic emptiness. Marsha Linehan's (1993) biosocial model proposes that BPD arises from the transaction between a biological vulnerability to emotional reactivity (heightened sensitivity, intense responses, slow return to baseline) and an invalidating developmental environment (caregivers who chronically dismiss, punish, or pathologise emotional expression). The child learns neither to label and modulate emotions nor to trust their internal experience, producing the adult presentation.

Aetiological evidence converges on early adversity. The longitudinal Children in the Community Study (Johnson et al., 1999) found childhood maltreatment quadrupled risk of PD diagnosis in early adulthood. Twin studies estimate BPD heritability at approximately 40%, with gene-environment interactions implicated. Recent neuroimaging research (Schulze et al., 2019) documents amygdala hyperreactivity and reduced prefrontal regulatory control consistent with the biosocial model.

Antisocial Personality Disorder and Psychopathy

ASPD describes a pervasive pattern of disregard for others' rights from age 15, with conduct disorder evidence before age 15. Hervey Cleckley's (1941) seminal monograph The Mask of Sanity identified the construct of psychopathy: superficial charm, absence of remorse, pathological lying, and shallow affect, often in individuals who do not meet ASPD's behavioural criteria. Robert Hare operationalised this with the Psychopathy Checklist-Revised (PCL-R; Hare, 1991), distinguishing interpersonal-affective traits (Factor 1) from antisocial-lifestyle features (Factor 2). The PCL-R has substantial predictive validity for institutional violence and recidivism but has been critically scrutinised for cultural and gender bias.

Narcissistic Personality Disorder: Kernberg vs Kohut

Two psychoanalytic accounts continue to shape NPD theory. Otto Kernberg conceptualises pathological narcissism as a defensive structure protecting against underlying envy, aggression, and a fragmented self; treatment involves transference-focused interpretation. Heinz Kohut, by contrast, viewed narcissism as arrested development arising from empathic failures in caregivers; treatment requires the therapist to provide the empathic mirroring the patient missed. Contemporary research distinguishes grandiose from vulnerable narcissism (Pincus & Lukowitsky, 2010), partly reconciling the historical disagreement.

Evidence-Based Treatments

Dialectical Behaviour Therapy (DBT; Linehan, 1993) combines cognitive-behavioural skills training (mindfulness, distress tolerance, emotion regulation, interpersonal effectiveness) with acceptance strategies; the largest randomised trials demonstrate reductions in self-harm and inpatient days. Mentalisation-Based Treatment (MBT; Bateman & Fonagy, 2004) targets the capacity to understand one's own and others' mental states; an 8-year follow-up demonstrated sustained gains. Schema Therapy (Young, 2003) integrates cognitive, behavioural, and experiential techniques to modify early maladaptive schemas; Giesen-Bloo et al. (2006) found it superior to transference-focused therapy on multiple outcomes. The most recent comparative meta-analysis (Storebo et al., 2020 Cochrane review) concludes that several psychotherapies outperform treatment-as-usual, with no clearly superior modality.

Stigma and Ethical Considerations

The BPS Division of Clinical Psychology's position has been consistent: PD diagnoses can be experienced as deeply invalidating, are applied inconsistently, and risk locating distress within the individual rather than addressing developmental and social causes. Lewis & Appleby (1988) demonstrated that the label 'personality disorder' alone reduced clinicians' willingness to engage therapeutically. Trauma-informed reformulations argue that many PD presentations are better conceptualised as adaptations to early trauma — a position partly reflected in the inclusion of complex PTSD in ICD-11. Clinical practice now increasingly emphasises formulation-based, recovery-oriented approaches alongside or in place of diagnostic labelling.

storyBeats.text: Dr. Chen opens with a single slide: a quote from a service-user advocacy group — 'I was a person with problems. Then I was given a personality disorder diagnosis, and I became a problem with a person.' She leaves the slide up for a long moment.

storyBeats.speaker: Dr. Chen
storyBeats.text: Personality disorder is the only DSM diagnosis where we are explicitly telling someone that the problem is not what they are experiencing — it is who they are. Think about that. It is the most stigmatising thing a clinician can say. Which is why the science has to be impeccable, and why ICD-11 moving to a dimensional model is, in my view, one of the most important reforms in modern psychiatry.
She pulls up Linehan's biosocial diagram: a triangle of biological vulnerability, invalidating environment, and the transactional loop between them.

storyBeats.speaker: Dr. Chen
storyBeats.text: Linehan is exceptional for two reasons. She built DBT on a coherent developmental theory rather than a list of symptoms to suppress. And she disclosed, eventually, that she had received a BPD diagnosis herself. The clinician and the theorist were also the survivor. That kind of integration is rare in our field.

storyBeats.speaker: Dr. Chen
storyBeats.text: The Johnson et al. 1999 longitudinal data are sobering. Childhood maltreatment quadruples risk of personality disorder diagnosis. If we are going to keep using these categories, we have an ethical obligation to read them as developmental records, not as moral verdicts.

storyBeats.speaker: Dr. Chen
storyBeats.text: And on treatment — when you read the Storebo 2020 Cochrane review, the headline is not that DBT beats MBT or schema therapy. It is that structured, theoretically coherent psychotherapy beats treatment-as-usual. Common factors do enormous work. Hold that in mind when you encounter the next 'breakthrough' therapy.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Guided Practice — Applying Linehan's Biosocial Model

Scenario: Alessia is a 24-year-old presenting to a community mental health team after a third hospital admission for self-harm. She describes feeling 'empty all the time', oscillating between idealising her therapist and feeling 'completely abandoned' when sessions end. Her case notes describe a childhood in which her emotional reactions were met with statements such as 'stop being dramatic' and 'you're making everyone's life harder'.

Using Linehan's (1993) biosocial model of borderline personality disorder, analyse Alessia's presentation. In your answer, define both components of the biosocial model, explain how the transaction between them might account for her current presentation, and briefly outline how DBT would target the resulting deficits.

subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
Linehan’s (1993) biosocial model proposes that BPD arises from the transaction between a biological vulnerability to emotion dysregulation (high sensitivity, intense reactivity, and a slow return to baseline) and an invalidating developmental environment.

Alessia's childhood experiences—being told to "stop being dramatic" or that she was "making everyone's life harder"—exemplify this invalidation. Her emotional expressions were dismissed and punished. Consequently, she did not learn to accurately label, understand, or modulate her emotions. Her current presentation—chronic emptiness, intense fear of abandonment, and self-harm—represents maladaptive attempts to regulate overwhelming affect in the absence of learned internal coping skills.

Dialectical Behaviour Therapy (DBT) directly targets these deficits by combining validation (accepting her current experience) with structured skills training in emotion regulation, distress tolerance, and interpersonal effectiveness, replacing self-harm with adaptive coping strategies.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
Independent Practice — Categorical vs Dimensional Models of Personality Disorder

The DSM-5 retains a categorical model of personality disorders, organising them into ten diagnoses across three clusters. ICD-11 has taken the more radical step of abandoning categorical diagnoses entirely, replacing them with a severity-based dimensional system. This disagreement between two major classification systems is unprecedented in modern psychiatry and raises fundamental questions about how the field should conceptualise enduring patterns of psychological difficulty.

Critically evaluate the categorical and dimensional approaches to personality disorder classification. In your answer, identify the empirical and conceptual problems with the DSM-5 categorical model, summarise the alternative offered by the Five Factor Model and the ICD-11 dimensional approach, and consider the clinical, ethical, and research implications of moving to a dimensional system. Reach a reasoned conclusion about which approach better serves patients and the discipline.

Write at least 150 words in continuous paragraphs. Reference at least three named theorists or studies. Reach clear evaluative conclusions rather than merely describing each approach.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
The DSM-5 categorical model of personality disorder faces empirical and conceptual challenges that have become difficult to defend. Inter-rater reliability is poor for several categories (the DSM-5 field trials reported kappa coefficients of 0.21–0.54 for personality disorders). Diagnostic comorbidity is extensive: most individuals meeting criteria for one PD meet criteria for others, suggesting the categorical boundaries are arbitrary rather than naturally occurring. The arbitrary symptom-threshold structure (e.g., requiring five of nine borderline criteria) produces qualitatively similar individuals on either side of the diagnostic line, undermining the claim that PDs are discrete clinical entities.

Dimensional approaches address these problems directly. The Five Factor Model (Costa & McCrae, 1992) demonstrates that the same trait dimensions — neuroticism, extraversion, openness, agreeableness, conscientiousness — account for both normal and pathological personality, with PDs representing extreme positions on these continua. The DSM-5 Alternative Model (Section III) and, more decisively, ICD-11 (WHO, 2022), have operationalised this insight: ICD-11 abandons the categorical system entirely in favour of severity ratings supplemented by trait qualifiers, retaining only a borderline pattern specifier in response to clinical demand.

The implications are substantial. Clinically, dimensional models support nuanced formulation: a moderately severe presentation with high negative affectivity and disinhibition tells a clinician more than a single diagnostic label. For research, dimensional measurement increases statistical power and enables continuous predictor analyses. Ethically, dimensional approaches reduce the stigmatising 'all-or-nothing' character of categorical diagnosis — a concern emphasised by the BPS Division of Clinical Psychology and supported by Lewis & Appleby's (1988) finding that the label 'personality disorder' alone reduced clinicians' willingness to engage therapeutically.

The principal objections to dimensional models are pragmatic. Categorical labels are easier to communicate and to use for service eligibility. There is also a concern that severity ratings introduce subjectivity. However, recent psychometric work (Bach et al., 2017) demonstrates that dimensional instruments can achieve good reliability, and the categorical model's reliability is hardly a benchmark to defend.

The weight of evidence favours the dimensional approach. ICD-11's adoption is empirically and ethically warranted, and the DSM is likely to follow as Section III evidence accumulates.

subChunks.title: Eating Disorders & Body Image
subChunks.hookHtml:
Eating disorders carry the highest mortality rate of any psychiatric condition. Anorexia nervosa alone has a standardised mortality ratio approximately five times that of the general population, with roughly one in five deaths attributable to suicide. Yet these are also profoundly psychological disorders — emerging from the intersection of culture, family, biology, and individual cognition in ways that defy any single-level explanation.

For clinical psychology, eating disorders are a critical test case: they demand sophisticated formulation, multidisciplinary collaboration, and recognition that biological vulnerability, sociocultural pressure, and family dynamics interact dynamically. They also reveal how the field has progressed — from blaming families in the mid-twentieth century to today's transdiagnostic, evidence-based models.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
DSM-5 Categories of Eating Disorder

DSM-5 organises eating and feeding disorders into several distinct categories. Anorexia nervosa (AN) is characterised by restriction of energy intake leading to significantly low body weight, intense fear of weight gain, and disturbance in body weight or shape experience. Two subtypes are specified: restricting type and binge-eating/purging type. Bulimia nervosa (BN) involves recurrent binge eating accompanied by compensatory behaviours (vomiting, laxative misuse, excessive exercise) at least weekly for three months, with self-evaluation unduly influenced by body shape and weight. Binge eating disorder (BED), formally recognised as a diagnosis in DSM-5, involves recurrent binges without regular compensatory behaviours and is now the most prevalent eating disorder in many populations. Avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder (ARFID) describes eating disturbance with significant nutritional or psychosocial consequences, without body-image disturbance — typically presenting in childhood and historically misclassified. OSFED (other specified feeding or eating disorder) captures clinically significant presentations that do not meet full criteria for any specific disorder; it accounts for the majority of clinical eating disorder cases.

Epidemiology

The Hudson et al. (2007) National Comorbidity Survey-Replication produced one of the most cited US prevalence estimates: lifetime prevalence of 0.9% (AN), 1.5% (BN), and 3.5% (BED) in women, with men showing roughly one-third the rates. A more recent systematic review (Galmiche et al., 2019) covering studies published 2000–2018 reported pooled lifetime prevalence of any eating disorder at 8.4% in women and 2.2% in men — a substantially higher figure, partly reflecting broader DSM-5 criteria and improved detection. The widely cited gender disparity is real but partly reflects diagnostic and presentation bias: men are systematically underdiagnosed, and presentations differ (e.g., muscle-focused disordered eating in men).

Aetiology — A Multifactorial Model

No single explanation accounts for eating disorder onset. The field has converged on a multifactorial model integrating sociocultural, biological, family, and individual psychological factors.

Sociocultural factors: Stice's (2002) dual-pathway model identified internalisation of the thin ideal as the key sociocultural risk factor — exposure to media and peer pressure leads vulnerable individuals to internalise an unrealistic body ideal, producing body dissatisfaction and subsequent restrictive eating or bulimic pathways. Meta-analytic evidence (Grabe et al., 2008) confirms the prospective relationship between media exposure and body dissatisfaction, with contemporary research extending this to social media (Fardouly & Vartanian, 2016).

Biological factors: Bulik et al.'s (2006) twin study established substantial heritability for AN (approximately 56%) and BN (approximately 60%), with shared genetic risk across eating disorders. The first eating-disorder genome-wide association study (Watson et al., 2019) identified eight significant loci for AN, with genetic correlations extending beyond psychiatric disorders to metabolic and anthropometric traits — recasting AN as a 'metabo-psychiatric' disorder.

Family systems: Minuchin's (1978) psychosomatic family model proposed that AN emerges in families characterised by enmeshment, overprotectiveness, rigidity, and conflict avoidance. This account was influential but contributed to a damaging era of family-blaming. Contemporary research has rejected the causal claim while acknowledging that family functioning influences treatment outcomes — a crucial distinction.

Cognitive-behavioural theory: Fairburn's (1981) original CBT model identified over-evaluation of weight and shape as the maintaining cognitive distortion — the rest of the disorder follows from this central evaluative scheme. His transdiagnostic reformulation (Fairburn, 2008) extended this framework across eating disorders, identifying four maintenance mechanisms: clinical perfectionism, core low self-esteem, interpersonal difficulties, and mood intolerance. This model underpins CBT-Enhanced (CBT-E), the current frontline psychological treatment for adult eating disorders.

Body Image Research

Cash (2004) developed a comprehensive cognitive-behavioural model of body image, distinguishing perceptual body image (accuracy of size estimation), cognitive-evaluative body image (beliefs and judgements about one's body), and behavioural components (avoidance, checking). Body dissatisfaction is now recognised as a major risk factor for eating disorders but is itself associated with a range of psychological harms in non-clinical populations.

Neurobiological Findings

Kaye et al.'s (2009) influential review proposed that AN involves altered insula and ventral striatal function, producing aberrant interoceptive awareness and altered reward processing — particularly a failure of the typically rewarding properties of food. More recent neuroimaging (Frank et al., 2018) extends this to dopamine-mediated learning differences in AN, suggesting that restriction may become self-reinforcing through altered prediction-error signalling.

Treatment Evidence

CBT-Enhanced (Fairburn, 2008) is the recommended first-line treatment for adult eating disorders other than AN, with randomised evidence supporting its effectiveness across diagnostic categories. Family-Based Treatment (FBT; Lock & Le Grange, 2013), also known as the Maudsley model, is the leading evidence-based treatment for adolescent AN, mobilising parents as the primary agents of weight restoration. MANTRA (Maudsley Anorexia Nervosa Treatment for Adults; Schmidt et al., 2015) targets cognitive-interpersonal maintaining factors specific to adult AN and has demonstrated comparable outcomes to specialist supportive clinical management in a multi-site RCT. Olanzapine has limited adjunctive evidence for AN; pharmacological treatment plays a more substantial role in BN (fluoxetine has FDA approval).

Mortality and Recovery

Arcelus et al.'s (2011) meta-analysis estimated a crude mortality rate of 5.1 deaths per 1,000 person-years for AN — substantially higher than for most psychiatric conditions. Recent long-term follow-up (Eddy et al., 2017) is more optimistic, finding that approximately two-thirds of women with AN and three-quarters with BN had achieved sustained recovery at 22 years — but the trajectory is often protracted, and a significant minority remain chronically affected.

storyBeats.speaker: Dr. Chen
storyBeats.text: Eating disorders kill more people than any other psychiatric condition. We have to start there because it is too easy, in academic writing, to treat AN as a fascinating cognitive case. It is also the leading cause of death for young women in some clinical samples. Both things are true.
She pulls up a comparison: Minuchin's 1978 psychosomatic family diagram alongside the 2015 AED position statement explicitly rejecting parent-blaming.

storyBeats.speaker: Dr. Chen
storyBeats.text: Minuchin's model was clinically generative — it took eating disorders seriously when they were ignored, and it pointed at the family system at a time when individual pathology was the default. But the causal claim that families cause AN was wrong, and it produced decades of harm. Today we mobilise families as the most powerful resource for adolescent recovery. Same observation, completely different theoretical frame.

storyBeats.speaker: Dr. Chen
storyBeats.text: Fairburn's transdiagnostic move in 2008 was conceptually elegant. Rather than separate treatments for AN, BN, and BED, he identified the shared maintenance mechanisms — over-evaluation of weight and shape, plus four broader factors. The treatment, CBT-E, works across diagnostic categories. That is exactly the kind of cumulative theory development we should aspire to.

storyBeats.speaker: Dr. Chen
storyBeats.text: And Watson et al.'s 2019 GWAS deserves real attention. Genetic correlations between AN and metabolic traits suggest we may have misunderstood the disorder for a century. It might be a metabo-psychiatric condition, not a primarily psychological one. The implications for treatment have not yet been worked out — but the data are striking.

She also reports difficulty managing low mood and frequent interpersonal conflict.

Guidance: Name the central evaluative scheme and the four maintenance mechanisms before applying them. Aim for 110–130 words.
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
According to Fairburn’s (2008) transdiagnostic model, the central maintaining cognitive distortion in Talia's presentation is the *over-evaluation of weight and shape*, which originated from her early adolescence bullying and now drives her binge-purge cycle.

Her presentation is further maintained by Fairburn’s four broader mechanisms: *clinical perfectionism* (evident in her academic striving, which likely generalises to rigid dietary rules); *core low self-esteem* (increasing her reliance on weight as her sole metric of worth); *mood intolerance* (using bingeing and purging to regulate her reported low mood); and *interpersonal difficulties* (frequent conflicts that likely trigger emotional distress).

CBT-Enhanced (CBT-E) would target these by simultaneously addressing the core eating disorder psychopathology (e.g., self-monitoring, establishing regular eating patterns to disrupt bingeing) while using specific modules to tackle perfectionism, enhance interpersonal effectiveness, and improve emotion regulation skills.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
Independent Practice — Sociocultural vs Biological Models of Eating Disorder Aetiology

For decades, eating disorders were understood primarily through sociocultural lenses: the thin ideal, media influence, and Western beauty standards were treated as the central causes. The Stice (2002) dual-pathway model and the explosion of social media research have continued this tradition. More recently, large-scale genetic studies — most notably the Bulik et al. (2006) twin study and Watson et al.'s (2019) genome-wide association study identifying eight loci for anorexia and shared genetic architecture with metabolic traits — have challenged the field to take biological aetiology far more seriously.

Critically evaluate the sociocultural and biological accounts of eating disorder aetiology. Consider the strengths and limitations of each, the empirical evidence supporting them, and how a contemporary biopsychosocial model integrates both. Reach a reasoned conclusion about the appropriate weighting of these factors in clinical formulation and public health intervention.

Write at least 150 words in continuous paragraphs. Reference at least three named studies. Reach evaluative conclusions rather than merely listing factors.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
Sociocultural accounts have made eating disorder research relevant to public health. Stice's (2002) dual-pathway model demonstrated that internalisation of the thin ideal — internalisation, not mere exposure — predicts body dissatisfaction, which in turn drives restrictive and bulimic pathways. Grabe et al.'s (2008) meta-analysis confirmed the prospective media-exposure-to-body-dissatisfaction relationship, and Fardouly & Vartanian's (2016) review extended this to image-based social media, where appearance comparison processes are amplified. These accounts explain the dramatic rise in body dissatisfaction across cohorts, gender differences in presentation, and the geographical distribution of eating disorders historically associated with Western, industrialised nations.

However, sociocultural models alone cannot explain why only a minority of individuals exposed to identical cultural pressures develop eating disorders, the substantial heritability evident in twin data, or the cross-cultural occurrence of AN-like presentations even in pre-globalisation samples. They also struggle to account for the chronicity and treatment resistance of AN specifically.

Biological accounts have closed this explanatory gap. Bulik et al.'s (2006) twin study established heritability estimates of 56% for AN and 60% for BN, comparable to schizophrenia and bipolar disorder. Watson et al.'s (2019) GWAS identified eight significant loci for AN and — most strikingly — found genetic correlations extending to metabolic and anthropometric traits including body mass index, type 2 diabetes risk, and insulin resistance. This recasts AN as a 'metabo-psychiatric' disorder, suggesting that biological predisposition involves not only psychological vulnerability but also altered energy homeostasis. Kaye et al.'s (2009) review of neurobiological findings in AN converges on altered insula and ventral striatal function, with implications for interoceptive awareness and reward processing.

The contemporary biopsychosocial position holds that biological vulnerability sets the stage, sociocultural pressure provides the trigger, and psychological mechanisms (over-evaluation of weight and shape; perfectionism) maintain the disorder. Stice's model is best read as describing one common developmental pathway among several, operating in genetically and metabolically vulnerable individuals. For clinical formulation, both levels of explanation should appear; for public health intervention, sociocultural targets (media literacy, social media moderation) remain important precisely because they may protect vulnerable individuals from triggering experiences they would otherwise be poorly equipped to withstand.

subChunks.title: Substance Use & Addictive Behaviours
subChunks.hookHtml:
Addiction has resisted every simple explanation it has been given. It is not a moral failure (despite the moral language that pervaded twentieth-century policy), nor purely a brain disease (despite the explanatory power of mesolimbic neuroscience), nor merely a learned habit (despite the relevance of conditioning principles). It is all of these things and more — a phenomenon that requires neurobiological, psychological, social, and cultural levels of analysis simultaneously.

For clinical psychology, addiction is the paradigm case for integrative thinking. It is also where evidence-based practice has produced some of its most consequential interventions — and where, in the last decade, psychedelic-assisted therapy has reopened a research line many considered permanently closed.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
DSM-5 Substance Use Disorder Criteria

DSM-5 abandoned the DSM-IV distinction between substance abuse and substance dependence, combining them into a single substance use disorder (SUD) diagnosis with severity ratings (mild, moderate, severe). Eleven criteria are listed across four clusters: impaired control (taking more than intended; unsuccessful attempts to cut down; time spent obtaining/using/recovering; craving); social impairment (failure to fulfil major role obligations; continued use despite interpersonal problems; activities given up); risky use (use in hazardous situations; continued use despite knowledge of consequences); pharmacological criteria (tolerance; withdrawal). Two or more criteria are required for diagnosis; severity is graded by criterion count.

Neurobiological Models

The mesolimbic dopamine system — projecting from the ventral tegmental area to the nucleus accumbens and prefrontal cortex — has been the dominant neurobiological focus. All major drugs of abuse acutely increase dopamine release in this pathway, though through different mechanisms (cocaine blocks dopamine reuptake; opioids disinhibit dopaminergic neurons; nicotine activates nicotinic acetylcholine receptors on those neurons).

Robinson & Berridge's (1993) incentive sensitisation theory is the most influential contemporary refinement. They argue that repeated drug exposure sensitises (rather than habituates) the neural systems that attribute incentive salience to stimuli — producing a dissociation between 'wanting' (incentive salience, mediated by mesolimbic dopamine) and 'liking' (hedonic experience, mediated by opioid and other systems). This explains why addicted individuals often continue using substances they no longer enjoy, and why drug-related cues retain their pull years after cessation. The theory has been extended (Berridge & Robinson, 2016) and is supported by extensive animal and human neuroimaging evidence.

Psychological Models

Operant conditioning frameworks distinguish positive reinforcement (drug use produces euphoria, increasing future probability of use) from negative reinforcement (drug use removes aversive states — withdrawal, anxiety, low mood — increasing future probability of use). Negative reinforcement becomes increasingly central as addiction progresses; Koob & Le Moal's (1997) opponent-process model integrates this with neurobiological data on stress-system recruitment in chronic addiction.

Classical conditioning accounts emphasise the role of drug-related cues. Stewart, de Wit & Eikelboom (1984) proposed that drug-conditioned stimuli (paraphernalia, locations, drug-using companions) come to elicit conditioned responses — including craving and physiological preparation for drug effects — through Pavlovian processes. This explains the high relapse rate when cessation is attempted without changing the cue environment.

Stages of Change

Prochaska & DiClemente's (1983) transtheoretical model identifies five stages: precontemplation (no intention to change), contemplation (considering change), preparation (planning change), action (active change), and maintenance (sustaining change beyond six months). The model emphasises that motivational state, not access to treatment, is often the critical determinant of progress, and that interventions should be matched to stage.

Motivational Interviewing

Building on these insights, Miller & Rollnick (2013) developed motivational interviewing (MI) — a directive but non-confrontational counselling style that elicits and strengthens the client's own arguments for change. MI is based on the recognition that traditional confrontational approaches paradoxically increase resistance to change. The core spirit of MI (partnership, acceptance, compassion, evocation) and core processes (engaging, focusing, evoking, planning) have been operationalised and extensively trialled. Meta-analytic evidence (Lundahl et al., 2010) supports moderate effects across substance use targets, with effects sustained for at least one year.

Behavioural Addictions

DSM-5 introduced gambling disorder as the first formally recognised behavioural addiction. The WHO went further: ICD-11 (2018) recognised gaming disorder as a diagnosable condition, characterised by impaired control, increasing priority given to gaming, and continuation despite negative consequences. This recognition was controversial — critics argued it medicalises a common recreational activity — but is supported by neuroimaging evidence of mesolimbic activation patterns analogous to substance addictions.

Cognitive Bias Modification

Wiers et al.'s (2011) cognitive bias modification (CBM) approach targets the implicit cognitive biases (approach bias toward substance-related stimuli; attentional bias to drug cues) that maintain addiction. In a randomised trial of alcohol-dependent patients, computerised approach-bias retraining added to standard CBT significantly improved one-year abstinence rates. Subsequent work has produced more mixed results (Boffo et al., 2019), but CBM remains a theoretically important illustration of how implicit cognitive processes can be experimentally modified.

Pharmacological Treatments

Several pharmacological agents have substantial evidence bases. Naltrexone (an opioid antagonist) reduces alcohol craving and consumption; methadone and buprenorphine (opioid agonist/partial agonist therapies) are the most effective interventions for opioid use disorder, with strong evidence for reduced mortality and improved retention in treatment. Disulfiram produces aversive reactions with alcohol but has limited evidence except in supervised settings. The integration of pharmacological and psychosocial treatment is the modern standard of care.

Recovery Models and Harm Reduction

Best & Lubman's (2012) work has been central to the move from a deficit-focused, abstinence-only model toward a recovery-oriented framework emphasising the rebuilding of identity, social capital, and meaning. This complements rather than replaces clinical treatment. The harm reduction philosophy — exemplified by needle exchanges, supervised consumption sites, opioid agonist therapy, and drug checking services — prioritises reducing the harms of substance use rather than requiring abstinence as a precondition for engagement. Evidence for harm reduction in opioid use disorder is robust; political controversy persists despite the evidence.

Psychedelic-Assisted Therapy

Psychedelic-assisted therapy has re-emerged as a serious research line. Bogenschutz & Johnson's (2016) review summarised the early modern evidence for psilocybin in addiction treatment, including a small open-label trial showing significant reductions in alcohol consumption. Davis et al.'s (2021) JAMA Psychiatry randomised trial of psilocybin-assisted therapy for major depression — while not a substance-use trial — has been formative in establishing the modern paradigm of supervised, dose-controlled psilocybin sessions paired with structured psychological preparation and integration. Substance use trials are ongoing; methodological challenges (blinding, expectancy effects) remain significant.

storyBeats.text: If you remember nothing else from this session, remember the wanting-liking dissociation. storyBeats.text: Naltrexone, methadone, and buprenorphine save lives. The evidence on opioid agonist therapy reducing overdose mortality is among the strongest in psychiatric medicine. Yet in many jurisdictions these treatments are stigmatised or restricted on moral rather than empirical grounds. Clinical psychology has a role in advocacy, not only practice.

storyBeats.text: The psychedelic research is genuinely interesting, and the methodological challenges are real. Blinding is essentially impossible — participants know whether they have received psilocybin. Expectancy effects are enormous. subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
Karim is currently in the *precontemplation* stage of Prochaska & DiClemente’s (1983) transtheoretical model, meaning he has no intention to change and does not view his drinking as problematic.

Direct confrontation is strongly contraindicated here. Miller & Rollnick (2013) demonstrate that confronting denial directly paradoxically increases resistance, forcing the client to defend their behaviour and entrenching their position.

Instead, an intervention consistent with Motivational Interviewing (MI) would embody a spirit of partnership and acceptance. The clinician would use open-ended questions and reflective listening to explore Karim’s experiences without judgement. The goal is to gently evoke "change talk"—helping Karim explore the discrepancies between his current behaviour and his broader life values (e.g., his relationship with his wife or his physical health), moving him toward the contemplation stage without triggering defensive resistance.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
Independent Practice — Incentive Sensitisation vs Negative Reinforcement Accounts

Robinson & Berridge's (1993) incentive sensitisation theory and Koob & Le Moal's (1997) opponent-process / negative reinforcement framework offer different but partly complementary accounts of addiction. The first locates the core pathology in the sensitisation of wanting-mediating neural systems, dissociable from hedonic liking. The second locates it in the recruitment of stress and anti-reward systems that progressively shift drug use from pleasure-seeking to discomfort-avoidance. Both have substantial neurobiological evidence; both have been used to justify different treatment emphases.

Critically evaluate these two accounts. Consider their distinctive empirical predictions, the evidence supporting each, their treatment implications, and whether they should be viewed as competing or complementary. Reach a reasoned conclusion about how a contemporary clinical psychologist should integrate them in formulation.

Write at least 150 words in continuous paragraphs. Reference at least three named studies. Reach evaluative conclusions, not merely description.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
Robinson & Berridge's (1993) incentive sensitisation theory makes a striking and counter-intuitive prediction: repeated drug exposure increases the incentive salience attributed to drug-related stimuli even as hedonic enjoyment may decline. This 'wanting without liking' dissociation is supported by elegant animal-model evidence, human neuroimaging of cue-elicited mesolimbic activation in abstinent users, and clinical observation that craving and drug-seeking can persist years after cessation, often outlasting any conscious desire to use. The theory's clinical contribution is to recast craving as a sensitised pathological process — not a sign of weak motivation or insufficient commitment to recovery — and to support cue-exposure and cognitive bias modification approaches (Wiers et al., 2011) that target the implicit appetitive processes directly.

Koob & Le Moal's (1997) opponent-process / negative reinforcement account emphasises a different mechanism: as addiction progresses, the brain's stress and anti-reward systems are progressively recruited, producing an aversive 'dark side' of withdrawal-related dysphoria, anxiety, and irritability. Substance use shifts from positive reinforcement (seeking pleasure) to negative reinforcement (escaping discomfort). The empirical support includes corticotropin-releasing factor and dynorphin upregulation in chronic users, the role of withdrawal-state distress in relapse, and the clinical observation that established addiction is characterised more by avoidance of an aversive baseline than by pursuit of euphoria.

These accounts are best understood as complementary rather than competing. Incentive sensitisation explains the persistence of cue-driven craving and the dissociation between wanting and liking. The negative reinforcement model explains why established addiction looks so different from initial recreational use and accounts for the central role of withdrawal-mediated relapse. A contemporary clinical formulation should integrate both: in early stages, positive reinforcement and incentive sensitisation may dominate; in established addiction, both processes contribute alongside negative reinforcement and stress-system recruitment.

The treatment implications are correspondingly broad. Cue-exposure, cognitive bias modification, and contingency management target the appetitive system; opioid agonist therapy and stress-management interventions target the negative-reinforcement processes; motivational interviewing (Miller & Rollnick, 2013) addresses the volitional and identity dimensions that neither neurobiological model fully captures. The most effective clinical psychology recognises that addiction is multi-systemic, and formulates accordingly.

subChunks.title: OCD, PTSD & Trauma-Related Disorders
subChunks.hookHtml:
Obsessive-compulsive disorder and the trauma-related disorders share a distinctive psychological architecture: the mind producing intrusive, distressing material — thoughts, images, memories — and the person organising their life around managing or suppressing it. The strategies that emerge are often the precise mechanisms that maintain the disorder, locking the system in a self-perpetuating loop.

Modern cognitive models have transformed how we understand and treat these conditions. They have done so not by replacing biological accounts but by specifying precisely how cognition, emotion, and behaviour interact to produce suffering — and, crucially, how those interactions can be deliberately altered.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
OCD Diagnostic Criteria

DSM-5 reclassified obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) into its own chapter, recognising the limitations of grouping it with anxiety disorders. OCD is characterised by obsessions (recurrent, persistent, intrusive thoughts, images, or urges experienced as unwanted and distressing) and compulsions (repetitive behavioural or mental acts performed to reduce distress or prevent feared outcomes). Diagnosis requires that obsessions or compulsions are time-consuming (>1 hour daily) or cause clinically significant distress or impairment. Common presentations include contamination/washing, harm/checking, symmetry/ordering, and forbidden/taboo thoughts (sexual, religious, aggressive) — the last often hidden from clinicians due to shame.

Salkovskis's Cognitive Model of OCD

Paul Salkovskis's (1985) cognitive model represents a major advance in understanding OCD. The key insight: intrusive thoughts themselves are virtually universal. Rachman & de Silva (1978) demonstrated that approximately 90% of non-clinical participants reported intrusive thoughts essentially identical in content to clinical obsessions. What distinguishes OCD is not the occurrence of the intrusion but the appraisal of its meaning. The clinical individual interprets intrusions as personally significant, as evidence of underlying badness, or as carrying a moral responsibility to prevent harm.

Salkovskis (1999) extended this with the concept of inflated responsibility — the belief that one has pivotal influence over outcomes, that failure to prevent harm is morally equivalent to causing harm, and that one's actions or thoughts can have a special potency to cause negative events. This appraisal pattern drives the compulsive behaviour: if I am responsible for preventing harm, and my intrusion suggests harm is possible, I must act to neutralise the risk. Compulsions are negatively reinforced by short-term anxiety reduction; long-term, they prevent the disconfirmation of threat beliefs and strengthen the appraisal that the intrusions were dangerous.

Thought-Action Fusion

Shafran, Thordarson & Rachman (1996) operationalised thought-action fusion (TAF) — the belief that thoughts and actions are morally or causally equivalent. Likelihood TAF: thinking about a negative event makes it more likely to occur. Moral TAF: thinking about a forbidden act is morally equivalent to performing it. TAF is elevated in OCD compared with anxious and non-clinical controls, and prospectively predicts OCD symptom course. The construct integrates Salkovskis's responsibility theory with broader cognitive-psychological work on metacognition.

Exposure and Response Prevention

Foa & Kozak's (1986) emotional processing theory provided the theoretical foundation for the most effective psychological treatment of OCD: exposure and response prevention (ERP). They argued that fear is represented as a structure in memory containing stimulus, response, and meaning information; pathological fear involves erroneous meaning associations; and corrective learning requires emotional activation (to access the fear structure) plus information incompatible with the existing structure (provided by repeated exposure without escape). For OCD, this means deliberate exposure to feared stimuli or intrusions while refraining from compulsions — allowing the prediction that harm will follow to be disconfirmed. ERP has substantial RCT evidence (Olatunji et al., 2013 meta-analysis); recent enhancements integrate cognitive techniques targeting appraisals (Wilhelm et al., 2009).

PTSD Criteria: DSM-5 vs ICD-11

The DSM-5 criteria for posttraumatic stress disorder require exposure to actual or threatened death, serious injury, or sexual violence, followed by symptoms across four clusters: intrusion (intrusive memories, dreams, flashbacks), avoidance (of trauma reminders), negative alterations in cognition and mood (negative beliefs, persistent negative emotional state, anhedonia, detachment), and arousal/reactivity (irritability, hypervigilance, exaggerated startle, sleep disturbance), persisting >1 month.

ICD-11 (WHO, 2018) made a deliberate move toward a narrower, more specific PTSD construct centred on three core symptom clusters: re-experiencing in the present (not merely intrusive memories — the experience of the trauma occurring now), avoidance of trauma reminders, and persistent sense of current threat (manifested as hypervigilance and enhanced startle). The narrower criteria produce somewhat lower prevalence estimates but arguably higher specificity.

Brewin et al.'s Dual Representation Theory

Brewin, Dalgleish & Joseph (1996) proposed a dual representation theory of PTSD, distinguishing two memory systems. Verbally accessible memories (VAMs) are consciously retrievable, contextualised, integrated with autobiographical memory. Situationally accessible memories (SAMs) contain sensory and physiological elements, are not consciously retrievable in the same way, and are triggered by environmental cues — accounting for flashbacks and the experiential 'reliving' quality of trauma memories. PTSD reflects an imbalance in which SAMs dominate and verbally accessible representations are poorly elaborated. Treatment must facilitate verbal elaboration of trauma memories to enable SAM material to be integrated rather than re-experienced.

Ehlers & Clark Cognitive Model

Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model has been particularly influential clinically. They propose that PTSD persists when individuals process the trauma in a way that produces a sense of current threat. Two processes are central: (1) negative appraisals of the trauma and its sequelae ('I am responsible', 'The world is dangerous', 'I am broken'); (2) the nature of the trauma memory — poorly elaborated, fragmented, and disconnected from contextual information, producing involuntary re-experiencing. Maladaptive coping strategies (rumination, thought suppression, safety behaviours) maintain both processes. Treatment (trauma-focused CBT) targets appraisals, elaborates the trauma memory, and modifies maintaining behaviours. NICE guidelines (2018) recommend Ehlers & Clark's protocol as a first-line PTSD treatment.

Complex PTSD

Judith Herman's (1992) clinical writings argued that prolonged, repeated trauma (childhood abuse, prolonged captivity, severe domestic violence) produces a distinctive symptom pattern beyond classic PTSD — including disturbances in self-organisation, affect regulation difficulties, and interpersonal disturbances. After decades of debate, ICD-11 formally recognised complex PTSD (CPTSD) as a distinct diagnosis, with three additional symptom clusters beyond core PTSD: affect dysregulation, negative self-concept, and disturbed relationships. Karatzias et al.'s (2017) ITQ validation study supported the empirical separability of CPTSD from PTSD in trauma-exposed samples.

Treatment Approaches

Trauma-focused CBT — including the Ehlers & Clark protocol and Cohen, Mannarino & Deblinger's (2006) TF-CBT for children — has the strongest evidence base. Eye Movement Desensitisation and Reprocessing (EMDR; Shapiro, 1989) involves recall of trauma material while making lateral eye movements; meta-analyses find broadly comparable outcomes to trauma-focused CBT, though the mechanism remains disputed. Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) approaches target experiential avoidance and values-based action; the evidence base is growing but smaller than for first-line treatments. Dissociative disorders — particularly dissociative identity disorder — remain controversial both in diagnostic validity and treatment, with the trauma model and the sociocognitive model offering different aetiological accounts.
